sources: Standard algebraic notation: the FIDE Laws of Chess, Appendix C [R], not re-read in this session
Descriptive notation of older books [R]; the aloud-reading idea is [H], untested here
docs/lesson-depth-standard.md (class A); docs/competition-chess-steps.md (short explanation, many exercises)

steps.text: You just played a written move. A **record** names two things: which piece moves, and the square where it lands. A pawn needs no letter, so a bare square name means a pawn moved there. The squares have the names you already know: file letter, then rank number. A game written as a list of records is a **score**.

steps.caption: A short score played from the start. Read each record first, then watch the move happen.

line.say: 1.e4: no letter, so a pawn moves, and it lands on e4.
1...e5: Black's pawn answers on e5. Still no letter, so still a pawn.
2.Nf3: N is the knight. It lands on f3 and now attacks the pawn on e5.
2...Nc6: Black's knight lands on c6 and defends the pawn on e5.
3.Bb5: B is the bishop. Its diagonal now points at the knight on c6.
3...a6: a pawn move again, so no letter. It attacks the bishop on b5 [I] and questions what White plans.

claims.statement: After Nf3 the knight attacks the pawn on e5.
After Bb5 the bishop attacks the knight on c6.
After a6 the black pawn attacks the bishop on b5.

steps.text: The other pieces get a capital letter in front of the square: **K** king, **Q** queen, **R** rook, **B** bishop, **N** knight. The knight borrows N because K is already the king. Try saying a record as a sentence: Nc3 is knight to c3. [H] Saying each record aloud this way may help you picture the move before you make it; test it on the next few.

Add an **x** when a piece is captured. For a piece, write its letter, then x, then the square: the bishop takes the knight on f6 is Bxf6. A pawn has no letter, so its capture starts with the file it came from. Two pawns may be able to take on the same square, and the file letter says which one.

steps.caption: Pawn captures start with a file letter. Watch which pawn takes each time.

line.say: 1.e4: a pawn to e4.
1...d5: Black's pawn answers and attacks the pawn on e4.
2.c4: a second white pawn. Now the pawns on c4 and e4 both attack d5.
2...e6: a second black defender of d5, so the pawn is guarded twice (pawn and queen).
3.cxd5: two pawns could take on d5, so the c says the c-pawn does it.
3...exd5: Black's e-pawn retakes. The record starts with the file it left, e.
4.exd5: now White's e-pawn takes. Same square, different file letter, different pawn.

claims.statement: After c4 two white pieces attack d5.
After e6 two black pieces defend d5.

steps.text: A **+** after a record means the move gives check. A **#** means checkmate, so the game ends. Neither mark changes which piece moves or where it lands; each only reports what the move did. Watch for the + on the next board, and for the # on the one after it.

steps.caption: A check is written with a +. Black must deal with it at once.

line.say: 1.e4: a pawn to e4. It opens the diagonal for White's queen.
1...f6: Black's f-pawn steps forward and opens the diagonal from e8 to h5.
2.Qh5+: the queen lands on h5 and attacks the king on e8. The + says check.
2...g6: Black answers the check by blocking with a pawn. A + asks for an answer.

claims.statement: After Qh5 the queen attacks the king on e8: check.

steps.caption: White to move, and one record ends the game. Read it piece by piece.

line.say: 4.Qxf7#: Q is the queen, x is the capture on f7, # is checkmate. The king has no escape.

steps.text: Castling is one move that moves two pieces, so it has its own record. The king moves two squares and the rook goes to the square the king crossed. **O-O** means the short way, toward the h-file. **O-O-O** means the long way, toward the a-file. Use the capital letter O. It needs an unmoved king and rook and a safe path; the castling lesson covers that.

steps.caption: Short castling. Notice where the king and the rook end up.

line.say: O-O: the king moves two squares toward the h-file and the rook lands on f1, the square the king crossed. One record, two pieces.

claims.statement: White can castle toward the h-file.
The square g1 is empty before castling.

steps.caption: Long castling needs three empty squares between king and rook. Watch White clear them.

line.say: 1.d4: a pawn to d4. It opens a path for the queen and the bishop on c1.
1...d5: Black answers with a pawn to d5.
2.Nc3: the knight leaves b1, clearing one of the squares castling needs.
2...Nf6: Black's knight comes out toward the centre.
3.Bf4: the bishop leaves c1, clearing the next square.
3...e6: Black opens a path for the bishop on f8.
4.Qd2: the queen leaves d1, so b1, c1 and d1 are all empty.
4...Be7: Black's bishop steps out and Black will be ready to castle too.
5.O-O-O: castling the long way. The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1.

claims.statement: The first move, d4, is legal.

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank it must become another piece. The record gives the landing square, an equals sign and the new piece's letter. So a8=Q means the pawn lands on a8 and turns into a queen. The record can name a queen, a rook, a bishop or a knight. A queen is usually strongest [H], but the choice is yours.

steps.caption: A pawn one step from the last rank. Read the record, then watch.

line.say: a8=Q: the pawn lands on a8 and becomes a queen. The =Q names what it turned into.

claims.statement: The pawn can promote to a queen on a8.

steps.text: **Remember.** A record names the piece letter and the square where it lands; a pawn move is just the square. Add x for a capture, + for check and # for checkmate. O-O and O-O-O are the two castling moves, and a pawn reaching the last rank adds an equals sign and the new piece, like a8=Q. To read any record, ask: which piece, and which square?
